content:
Reasons Thunderbird might complain about the image:

- If it's stored in a place that it didn't have access to, like in \Program Files, or \Windows, or another of other locations protected by the OS.

- If it were in use by another program, including image viewers or editors.

- Similarly, it were being scanned by your Anti-Virus. Some of those are especially bad about letting go of the file once it's done, if it ever does.

- If you were dragging it from another program that was actually displaying a temporary copy that was deleted in the meantime. This could include dragging from one email to another.

- If you were experiencing disk corruption. This will happen to all hard disk drives eventually and you should keep an eye out for the signs, one of which is files that fail move and copy operations.

- Email services usually have message size limits. If you are attaching many large images, your email may be hitting that limit.


It's extremely unlikely that Thunderbird was "compromised" in a way that would result in this. Especially if you installed it from an installer downloaded from the official thunderbird.net source. Nobody would bother, even if they had access to the computer. It would be pointless.

content:
I can also confirm this issue. Windows 11 system with Thunderbird 152.0 (64-bit).

I used a completely new dummy profile and, to be on the safe side, changed the drafts folder path to “Local Folder.”

Here's what I noticed while testing with Procmon: 1. When clicking “Forward”, the attachments are automatically saved as “nstemp” files in the %TEMP% directory. 2. When the draft is saved for the first time, these files are immediately deleted, even though the email is still open at that point. 3. When saving for the second time, Thunderbird attempts to reload the nstemp files. These are no longer present at that point, which causes the error.

This is also visible in the error console.

This error also occurs when automatic saving is enabled. This is enabled by default and happens every 5 minutes.

Note I can also confirm that the problem only occurs when the “Forward Messages” setting is set to "Inline". However, this is because Thunderbird apparently handles attachments differently in this case and stores the forwarded email file in a subfolder named “pid-XXXXX” (where XXXXX is Thunderbird's current process ID) within the Temp folder.
